patients.summary: Retired math teacher who joined in 2017 with hypertension, stable schizophrenia on quetiapine, knee osteoarthritis and BPH after TURP. Primary adrenal insufficiency diagnosed in 2020, recurrent BPH, amlodipine edema, senile purpura, a Spigelian hernia and orthostatic hypotension follow; after his last visit he has an ED visit for urinary retention with post-renal AKI.

documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
70 yo retired high school math teacher, coming over after his longtime PCP retired. Brought his bottles in a shopping bag, which helped.

HTN: about ten years, on HCTZ 25 daily since the start. Doesn't check at home. No headaches, CP, SOB.

Schizophrenia: dx in his twenties, one hospitalization decades ago, none since. Stable on quetiapine 200 qhs from the community psychiatry clinic, sees them twice a year. Denies AH/VH today, organized and pleasant, a bit formal. He would like us not to change anything about that med, which is fine.

Knees: OA both knees per old records, aches with stairs and after long walks, manages without pills for now.

Prostate: TURP in February this year at an outside urology group after years of slow stream on medication. Says he voids "like a young man" since and stopped the urology pill afterward. Has not been back to them.

Aspirin 81 daily on his own for years, "for the heart." No hx MI, stroke or stents.

PMH as above. PSH: TURP 2017. Meds: HCTZ 25 daily, quetiapine 200 qhs, ASA 81. NKDA.
FH: father HTN and an enlarged prostate. Mother osteoporosis and macular degeneration. Sister with autoimmune thyroid disease. Paternal uncle type 1 diabetes.
SH: divorced, lives alone in an apartment, daughter lives ten minutes away and checks in. Smoked about a pack a day for 30 years, quit roughly 12 years ago. A drink or two a month. Walks most mornings.

Exam: well-appearing, NAD. BP 138/82. Lungs clear. Heart RRR, no murmur. Abd soft, NT, no masses. No edema. Knees with crepitus bilaterally, no effusion, full ROM. Skin unremarkable. Affect mildly flat, thought process linear.

A/P
1. HTN - ok on HCTZ. CMP.
2. Schizophrenia - stable, psychiatry manages. CMP, A1c and lipids yearly for quetiapine monitoring.
3. Knee OA - activity, consider acetaminophen if it worsens.
4. BPH s/p TURP - asymptomatic.
5. Former smoker, 30 pk-yr - qualifies for lung screening: LDCT ordered after shared decision talk. One-time aortic ultrasound ordered.
6. Health maintenance: Hep C ab, TSH, CBC today. Records request to old office for colonoscopy and vaccine history. Flu shot when it arrives.
RTC 6 months.

- BP readings 130s-140s/80s on HCTZ over several years.
- Psychiatry letters, stable on quetiapine.
Scanned to chart.

orders.reason: Fatigue, weight loss, hyperpigmentation, low AM cortisol

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Masked visit, screened at door.

S: about 2 months of steadily worse fatigue and poor appetite. Down from 80 kg in the fall to 74 today without trying. Lightheaded when he stands quickly, never passed out. Has noticed his forearms look tanned though he's barely been outside since March, which bothers him as a puzzle more than a worry. No N/V/abd pain, no fever, no cough, no melena. Sleep ok. Mood flat but not depressed by his account, no change in voices or thinking, psychiatry phone visit last month fine. Same meds.

O: BP 104/62, well below his usual. Weight 74 kg. Thin, tired-appearing. Forearms diffusely darker than upper arms, oral mucosa looks pigmented on the inner cheeks. Lungs clear, heart regular, abdomen soft, nontender. No LAD. No edema.

A/P
Fatigue, weight loss, low BP with darkening of skin and mucosa - this picture worries me for primary adrenal insufficiency. Drawing CMP, CBC and an AM cortisol now (drawn 8:20). Will call him with the cortisol and get him into endocrinology quickly if low. Hold off on HCTZ change until labs back. Reviewed red flags: vomiting, fainting, confusion -> ED and tell them about this workup.

documents.title: Lab results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Called pt. AM cortisol 2.8 mcg/dL, very low for 8 a.m.; CMP and CBC otherwise unremarkable. Explained this points toward the adrenal glands not making enough cortisol and that he needs endocrinology soon. Spoke with endocrinology triage: new-patient slot June 1, with stimulation testing that morning; they asked that we not start steroids before the test unless he gets sicker. Pt and daughter (on speaker) understand ED precautions. Daughter will drive him.

events.reason: Fatigue, weight loss, hyperpigmentation; low AM cortisol

medications.sig: Take 2 tablets (20 mg) by mouth every morning and 1 tablet (10 mg) every evening

documents.title: Endocrinology consultation
documents.author: endocrinology
documents.body:
Endocrinology consultation, date of service 06/01/2020. Received by fax 06/22.

Reason: low morning cortisol, referred by his primary care physician.

This 72-year-old man describes several months of increasing tiredness, reduced appetite and weight loss he did not intend. He feels faint on standing. His forearms have darkened although he has had little sun exposure this spring. He has hypertension on hydrochlorothiazide, schizophrenia on quetiapine, osteoarthritis and BPH treated by TURP in 2017. Aspirin 81 mg. NKDA. Former smoker.

Exam: BP 100/60. Diffuse hyperpigmentation over both forearms and on the buccal mucosa. Remainder unremarkable.

Data: CBC with eosinophils 23%. Cosyntropin 250 mcg IV: cortisol 2.6 mcg/dL at baseline and 4.1 mcg/dL at 60 minutes. Plasma ACTH 486 pg/mL.

Impression: primary adrenal insufficiency.

Plan: hydrocortisone 20 mg on waking and 10 mg in the late afternoon/evening; fludrocortisone 0.1 mg daily. Sick-day rules reviewed with patient and daughter: double the hydrocortisone for fever or significant illness, go to the ED for vomiting. Advised a medical alert bracelet. Follow-up here in 3 months and then yearly.

Allergies: NKDA.
cc: primary care

documents.title: Urology consultation
documents.author: urology
documents.body:
Urology office note, seen 6/11/2021, faxed 6/28.

Mr. Levine had a TURP with our group in 2017. For roughly six months he has had trouble starting his stream, a weaker flow and the sense that his bladder doesn't empty. No dysuria. He also carries a diagnosis of primary adrenal insufficiency, followed by endocrinology.

Abdomen soft, nontender, bladder not distended to palpation. DRE: prostate moderately enlarged, firm, nontender, no nodules.
Urinalysis unremarkable. Bladder scan post-void residual 150 mL.

Assessment: recurrent benign prostatic hyperplasia after TURP with obstructive symptoms.
Plan: tamsulosin 0.4 mg nightly after supper; warned about lightheadedness on standing, especially the first week. Recheck in 3 months by phone, sooner if unable to void.

Meds reviewed: hydrocortisone, fludrocortisone, hydrochlorothiazide, quetiapine, aspirin. Allergies: NKDA.

documents.title: Pill timing
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Urology gave me tamsulosin after supper. My evening hydrocortisone is also at supper. Is it all right to take them together or should I space them?

documents.title: RE: Pill timing
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Checked with the doctor: fine to take them at the same time. Keep the tamsulosin about half an hour after you eat, and stand up slowly in the evening.

reports.text: Complete transthoracic echocardiogram. Left ventricle normal in size with normal wall thickness and normal systolic function; estimated ejection fraction 60%. No regional wall motion abnormality. Right ventricle normal size and function. Atria normal size. Valves structurally normal without significant stenosis or regurgitation. No pericardial effusion. IVC normal with normal respiratory variation.
reports.conclusion: Normal left ventricular size and function, EF 60%. Normal study.

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
74 yo M with primary adrenal insufficiency and recurrent BPH, here 6 weeks after amlodipine was added to HCTZ.
BP response is good: home systolics now about 130, down from the 160s; 132 here (was 168 in Feb). Feels better overall.
But both ankles swell, painless, starting a couple of weeks after the new pill. Worse by evening, a little better in the morning. Socks leave marks.
No shortness of breath, chest pain, orthopnea or PND. No NSAIDs, and no steroids other than his replacement hydrocortisone/fludrocortisone at the usual doses.
Meds: amlodipine 5, HCTZ 25, ASA 81, hydrocortisone 20/10, fludrocortisone 0.1, tamsulosin 0.4, quetiapine 200 qhs, acetaminophen prn.

Vitals otherwise normal. JVP not elevated. Heart RRR, no murmur or gallop. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, no liver edge, no fluid wave. 2+ pitting edema both legs to above the ankles, symmetric, calves soft and nontender.
ECG in office: NSR, normal.
Echo from March reviewed: normal LV function.

A/P
Bilateral ankle edema, timing and pattern fit amlodipine (dihydropyridine effect), not heart failure: JVP, lungs and March echo normal. Checking CMP (kidneys, albumin) and BNP today.
Plan discussed: he doesn't want to give up the first real BP control he's had, and the swelling doesn't bother him much. Keep amlodipine 5, elevate legs in the evening, knee-high compression stockings (light). Re-evaluate at the wellness visit; if worse we'll switch agents.
HTN - improved on two agents.

orders.reason: Recurrent purple patches on hands and forearms

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Here with his daughter, who scheduled the visit. Over the past few months purple patches keep appearing on the backs of his hands and forearms after small knocks (car door, kitchen cabinet). Each fades over weeks. Not painful or itchy. No nosebleeds, gum bleeding, blood in urine or stool. On aspirin 81. No new meds.

Vitals as charted. Several flat purple patches, non-blanching, on the dorsal hands and extensor forearms, various ages. No petechiae elsewhere. No LAD, no spleen tip.

A/P
Bruising on sun-exposed, thin forearm skin - likely benign age-related fragility, possibly with his steroid replacement and aspirin, but checking CBC with platelets and PT/INR first. Daughter would like a dermatologist to look; referral placed and labs will go with it.

documents.title: Blood count and clotting
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Blood count, platelets and clotting test are all normal, so there is no bleeding disorder behind the bruises. I've sent the results to dermatology with the referral.

documents.title: Dermatology consultation
documents.author: dermatology
documents.body:
Dermatology clinic note, visit 06/05/2023 (received 07/11/2023).

75 y/o man with primary adrenal insufficiency since 2020, accompanied by his daughter. Several months of purple patches that come up after trivial bumps and fade over weeks to months. No pain, pruritus or bleeding.
Meds per referral: hydrochlorothiazide, amlodipine, hydrocortisone, fludrocortisone, tamsulosin, quetiapine, aspirin 81. NKDA.

Exam: several non-blanching violaceous ecchymoses over the extensor hands and forearms, no warmth, edema or tenderness. Remainder of the skin exam unremarkable.
Labs from referring office: CBC, coagulation studies and platelet count normal.

Impression: senile (actinic) purpura.
Plan: reassurance; long sleeves or forearm sleeves for protection, emollient for dry skin. No further workup. Follow up as needed.

documents.title: Dermatology visit
documents.author: patient
documents.body: This is his daughter writing on Dad's account. The skin doctor said the bruises are 'senile purpura', thin skin from age and sun, nothing dangerous, no treatment needed. She said to keep his arms covered. Just letting you know. Should he stop the baby aspirin?

documents.title: RE: Dermatology visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Thanks for the update, that matches what we thought. No need to change any medicines for this; arm sleeves are a good idea. We'll look for the dermatology letter.

documents.title: Annual Wellness Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
AWV.
Dermatology letter in: senile purpura, reassurance. Wearing sleeves.
BP fine at home. Ankles same. Voiding fine. Endocrinology yearly in spring, unchanged. Psychiatry unchanged.
No falls. Stopped driving at night. Independent.
PHQ-2 0. Recall 3/3, clock normal.

Vitals as charted. Scattered purpura on the forearms. 1+ ankle edema. Heart and lungs normal.

Plan: annual labs. Flu and updated COVID with nurse in October. RSV vaccine recommended at 75+, he'll get it at the pharmacy. Tdap due next year. RTC winter.

documents.title: Vaccines
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Flu L deltoid, 2023-24 COVID R deltoid. Bandage over a small bruise on the R arm from the stick, pressure held a little longer. Fine.

orders.reason: Reducible left lower quadrant abdominal wall bulge

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Noticed a soft lump low on the left side of his belly a few months back when getting out of bed. More obvious when he stands or bears down, gone when he lies flat. Doesn't hurt. Bowels regular, no nausea, appetite fine, weight steady. No injury, never had belly surgery, doesn't lift anything heavy.

Vitals as charted. Abdomen: soft, nontender. Standing, a soft bulge in the left lower quadrant lateral to the rectus, bigger with a cough, reduces easily with gentle pressure. No erythema. Not in the groin; inguinal canals normal.

A/P
Reducible LLQ abdominal wall hernia, likely lateral (Spigelian-type) location. No signs of incarceration. Referred to general surgery for an opinion. Reviewed warning signs: pain, a bulge that won't go back, vomiting -> ED.

events.reason: Left lower quadrant abdominal wall bulge

documents.title: General surgery consultation
documents.author: general surgery
documents.body:
General surgery consultation, seen 06/10/2024 (letter received 06/27/2024).

76-year-old man, known to our hospital system since 2020 for primary adrenal insufficiency, with recurrent BPH and hypertension, also osteoarthritis. A few months ago he noticed a swelling in the left lower abdomen on rising from bed, gradually more visible with standing or straining. No trauma, no prior abdominal operations, no heavy lifting. No pain, change in bowel habit, nausea or weight loss.
Allergies: NKDA.

Exam: soft, reducible mass in the left lower quadrant abdominal wall several centimeters lateral to the lateral edge of the rectus abdominis. Enlarges with strain, reduces with gentle pressure. No overlying erythema, no tenderness, no signs of obstruction.

Impression: left Spigelian hernia, reducible.

Plan: we discussed elective repair given the narrow neck these hernias typically have, against his age and the perioperative steroid coverage he would need. He would prefer to wait. Reasonable with clear return precautions: pain, a firm bulge that does not reduce, vomiting or inability to pass gas should prompt immediate evaluation. Happy to see him again to proceed with repair whenever he wishes.

documents.title: Hernia question
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Daughter here on Dad's account. The surgeon said he can wait on the hernia. What exactly should make us go to the emergency room? He forgets the list.

documents.title: RE: Hernia question
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Go in right away if the bulge becomes painful, gets firm and won't push back in when he lies down, or if he starts vomiting or can't pass gas. Also tell them about his adrenal insufficiency so he gets extra hydrocortisone. A copy of this is printable from the portal; it may help to put it on the fridge.

documents.title: Annual Wellness Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
AWV.
Surgery letter in: left Spigelian hernia, he chose to wait. Bulge unchanged, painless.
BP ok at home. Ankle swelling and arm bruising unchanged. Voiding ok. Endocrinology and psychiatry unchanged.
No falls. Still independent; daughter manages the bills now at his request.
PHQ-2 0. Recall 3/3.

Vitals as charted. Reducible LLQ bulge on standing, nontender. 1+ ankle edema. Heart and lungs normal.

Plan: annual labs. Flu and COVID next month. Hernia warning signs reviewed again. RTC winter.

documents.title: Vaccines
documents.author: RN
documents.body: High-dose flu (trivalent this season) and 2024-25 COVID given, one each arm. No problems.

documents.title: Refills
documents.author: MA
documents.body: New plan year; mail order needs new scripts. Sent amlodipine 5 mg #90 x3 and HCTZ 25 mg #90 x3. Pt overdue for winter visit, booked 2/12.

documents.title: Office Visit

Never sent the BP log.

events.reason: Frequency, nocturia, weak stream, incomplete emptying

documents.title: Urology follow-up
documents.author: urology
documents.body:
Urology clinic note, DOS 06/03/2025, sent 08/12/2025.
Known patient, TURP here years ago and on tamsulosin since 2021. Four months of recurrent frequency, nocturia, weak stream and incomplete emptying. No hematuria, no dysuria. BP 160/94 today; he says his blood pressure has been running high.
DRE: prostate symmetrically enlarged, smooth, nontender.
UA normal. Creatinine 1.0 mg/dL.
A/P: BPH, recurrent. Adding finasteride 5 mg daily to tamsulosin; explained it takes months to shrink the gland. Follow up in 6 months.
NKDA.

documents.title: New prescription fill
documents.author: pharmacy
documents.body: Fill history: finasteride 5 mg tablets #30 dispensed 06/03/2025, prescriber urology. Added to med list pending urology note.

documents.title: Annual Wellness Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
AWV. Turned 78 last month.
Urology note received: finasteride added in June. Stream "a little better, maybe." Up twice at night.
BP: no home log. Feels fine.
Hernia, purpura, ankle edema unchanged. Endocrinology in spring, same doses. Psychiatry same.
No falls. Independent at home, daughter helps with errands.
PHQ-2 0. Recall 2/3, clock normal.

Vitals as charted, BP again above goal. Heart, lungs normal. 1+ ankle edema. Reducible LLQ bulge.

Plan: annual labs. BP follow-up visit in 6-8 weeks with home readings. Flu and COVID next month.

documents.title: Dizziness
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Daughter called: for about a week Dad gets dizzy and nearly faints when he stands, vision goes blurry for a few seconds and his heart races, then it settles if he sits. Hasn't fallen or passed out. No chest pain, no vomiting, eating and drinking ok. Taking hydrocortisone as usual. Booked Monday 3/23 in person. Advised: sit on the edge of the bed before standing, fluids, ED if he faints, falls, has chest pain or can't keep pills down.

reports.text: Sinus rhythm, rate normal. Normal axis, PR, QRS and QT intervals. No ST-T abnormality. Unchanged from June 2022.
reports.conclusion: Normal sinus rhythm. No change from prior.

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Here with daughter. About 10 days of lightheadedness and near-fainting when he gets up, with blurred vision and a pounding heartbeat for a few seconds. Passes when he sits. No syncope, no falls, no chest pain or SOB. No vomiting or diarrhea. Not sick otherwise; taking hydrocortisone 20/10 and fludro daily, no missed doses per pill box. No new meds.

Seated BP 146/88. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear. 1+ ankle edema, unchanged. Neuro nonfocal.
ECG: NSR, unchanged from 2022.

A/P
Near-syncope on standing with palpitations in a 78 yo on tamsulosin, two antihypertensives and adrenal replacement. Wants a cardiology look given the palpitations; urgent referral placed. Until then: rise slowly, sit before standing, keep fluids up, stockings on. Daughter will stay with him more this week. ED precautions.

events.reason: Dizziness and near-fainting on standing, palpitations

documents.title: Cardiology consultation
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
Cardiology consult, seen 04/01/2026 (faxed 04/20).
Referred for two weeks of lightheadedness and near-fainting on standing, with blurred vision and palpitations. Primary adrenal insufficiency since 2020.
Meds: quetiapine 200 mg nightly, tamsulosin 0.4 mg, amlodipine 5 mg, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg, hydrocortisone 20/10 mg, fludrocortisone 0.1 mg, aspirin 81 mg. (Finasteride per PCP list.) NKDA.

Orthostatic vitals: seated BP 145/90, HR 78; standing BP 110/70, HR 98.
Exam otherwise unremarkable.
Labs: Hgb 14.2 g/dL, Na 140 mEq/L, K 4.1 mEq/L, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, fasting glucose 98 mg/dL.

Impression: orthostatic hypotension, likely multifactorial (alpha-blocker, thiazide diuretic, adrenal insufficiency, age). No evidence of structural or arrhythmic cause on today's evaluation; palpitations correspond to the compensatory rise in heart rate.
Recommendations: slow staged rising, adequate fluid and salt intake, waist-high compression if tolerated, avoid hot showers standing. No medication changes from our standpoint; would defer adjustments of his antihypertensives and replacement doses to primary care and endocrinology. Return as needed.

documents.title: Cardiology letter
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Cardiology note received and given to PCP. Called daughter: dizziness happening less since he started getting up slowly and wearing the stockings. Booked follow-up 5/22.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
F/u after cardiology. Their letter: orthostatic hypotension, multifactorial, non-drug measures, no med changes from them.
Since then: dizzy spells less often, maybe twice a week, brief, always on getting up fast. No falls or faints. Stockings most days, drinking more water. Up 2 times at night to void, stream so-so; on tamsulosin and finasteride. Hernia unchanged.

Seated BP 142/86. Heart regular, lungs clear, 1+ ankle edema.

A/P
Orthostatic hypotension - better with measures; keep doing them. Leaving meds as they are for now; will revisit once endocrinology has seen him this summer.
HTN - seated pressure above goal, standing drops: no intensification.
Adrenal insufficiency - BMP today.
Recurrent BPH - urology follow-up due, he will call them.
Return 3 months.

documents.title: Lab results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Your sodium, potassium and kidney numbers from Friday are normal. Keep up the fluids and slow standing.

procedures.procedure: Insertion of indwelling catheter into urinary bladder

documents.title: Emergency department note
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Emergency department provider note, 06/04/2026 (brief note faxed to PCP 06/08/2026).

CC: confusion, fatigue, decreased urine output x 2 days. Brought by daughter. Hx recurrent BPH (urology June 2025), TURP remotely, HTN, primary adrenal insufficiency on hydrocortisone/fludrocortisone, schizophrenia. Takes tamsulosin. Last BM 3 days ago.
NKDA.

VS within normal limits. Disoriented. Distended, palpable bladder.
Bedside bladder scan: 700 mL retained.
Cr 4.2 mg/dL (baseline 1.0), BUN 82 mg/dL. UA bland, no hematuria or proteinuria. FENa 0.8%.

MDM: acute kidney injury, post-renal, from bladder outlet obstruction with urinary retention.
Course: indwelling urethral catheter placed with drainage of retained urine. Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV given (stress dosing for adrenal insufficiency). Admitted to the medicine service for monitoring of renal recovery and post-obstructive diuresis.

documents.title: Dad was in the hospital
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Daughter writing. Dad was admitted last Thursday, his bladder wasn't emptying and his kidneys got backed up. He was very confused. He came home yesterday after 3 nights with a catheter in. They said his kidney number was 1.6 when he left and going down. Urology is supposed to see him in a couple of weeks. He's much clearer now. Do you need anything from us?

documents.title: RE: Dad was in the hospital
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Thank you for letting me know, and I'm glad he's clearer. We received the ED note but not the discharge paperwork; could you bring or photograph the discharge instructions and medication list? Keep the catheter bag below the bladder, plenty of fluids, and call for fever, no urine in the bag, or new confusion. Make sure he keeps taking his hydrocortisone; double it if he runs a fever. I'd like to see him after urology.

documents.title: Urology update
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Urology took the catheter out today and he passed the voiding test. They'll see him again later in the summer about the prostate. I couldn't find the discharge papers, sorry, I think they went home with the hospital bag that got thrown out.

documents.title: RE: Urology update
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Good news, thank you. We'll request the hospital records directly. Call to book a follow-up whenever he's up to it.

documents.title: Fill history
documents.author: pharmacy
documents.body: Fill history update: hydrocortisone 10 mg #90 (endocrinology), tamsulosin 0.4 mg #90 and finasteride 5 mg #90 (urology) dispensed 07/20/2026.

documents.title: Hospital records request
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: Second request faxed to the hospital's records department for the June admission discharge summary and labs; first request 7/1 not answered. Called daughter about booking the follow-up: she'll call once his urology date is set. Nothing booked.
